heading: Selected reservoir modelling engagements.
lead: Structured the way we hand work back to clients: the brief, the geological problem, how we modelled it, and what it changed about the field's development plan.

draftNote.text: LOG 01 is an illustrative placeholder pending client confirmation. LOG 02–05 are real — see each entry's badge and source note for its current status.

items.title: Natural-state and production-history calibration, high-enthalpy volcanic field
items.brief: Validate an updated equation-of-state formulation against 30+ years of well and production history before it was used for new development scenarios.
items.challenge: Steep topography and a shallow magmatic heat source produce strong lateral temperature gradients that simple models under-predict.
items.method: Multi-scenario natural-state and history-matched runs across the revised EOS, cross-checked against a combined-field simulation case.
items.outcome: Confirmed EOS fix carried through to production forecasts; resource risk range tightened for the client's development committee.
items.source: Related publication: Porras, E. & Xicara, J. (2020) — "A new numerical model of Amatitlán geothermal system, Guatemala", Proceedings, World Geothermal Congress 2020.

items.title: Desert Queen: natural-state modelling of a blind Nevada system
items.loc: Desert Queen Geothermal Prospect, Churchill County, Nevada · Blind system, no surface expression
items.brief: Build a natural-state numerical model of a classic blind Great Basin geothermal system, informed by decades of public exploration data and a structurally-controlled conceptual model, ahead of the same uncertainty quantification and resource-assessment workflow used at Tecuamburro–Infiernitos.
items.challenge: No fumarole, hot spring or surface expression exists at Desert Queen — the system was found entirely through temperature-gradient drilling, 2 m soil-temperature surveys and geophysics, so the natural-state model has to earn its match against subsurface data alone, with the up/outflow geometry itself as the main open question.
items.method: Structural and conceptual model built from public exploration history (Phillips Petroleum, the Great Basin Center for Geothermal Energy, Magma Energy, and Cyrq Energy/Raser Power Systems' own geologic mapping, gravity, magnetics, magnetotellurics, 2 m temperature survey and temperature-gradient wells) plus Dellerman's (2021) geothermal play-fairway analysis, now being carried into a calibrated numerical natural-state model.
items.outcome: In progress. The conceptual model places upflow where the Desert Queen fault zone terminates to the south-southwest and steps over to the Power Line fault, with ~140 °C measured at the hottest temperature-gradient well and a silica-geothermometer estimate near 168 °C (335 °F) for reservoir temperature. The natural-state model currently being built will test that picture numerically before UQ and resource assessment begin.
items.source: Public exploration history summarised from Dellerman, N.P. (2021) — "Application of Geothermal Play Fairway Analysis to the Desert Queen Geothermal Prospect, Northern Hot Springs Mountains, Churchill County, Nevada", MS thesis, University of Nevada, Reno (advisor J.E. Faulds), and Cyrq Energy/Raser Power Systems' Desert Queen Unit geologic reporting.

items.title: Combined development: Tecuamburro + Infiernitos, 25-year forecast
items.loc: Tecuamburro Volcanic Complex, Guatemala · Two-resource joint development
items.brief: Test whether developing Tecuamburro and Infiernitos as one combined project changes either resource's own forecast, using a framework where every combined-scenario sample shares the identical natural-state realisation, injection strategy and pump-sizing logic as its single-resource counterpart.
items.challenge: Determine whether joint development causes genuine resource-scale interaction — shared pressure support, competition for reinjection capacity — or whether independent forecasts simply sum, and prove it at the level of reservoir pressure itself rather than inferring it from power output alone.
items.method: 293-sample stochastic ensemble; automated well-siting growth algorithm; source-network-coupled reinjection in Waiwera; matched sample-by-sample against each resource's independent forecast; interference tested directly via per-sample reservoir pressure at Infiernitos' own feedzones.
items.outcome: Combined development changes each resource's own forecast by under 1% (Wasserstein-1 distance 0.13–0.38 MWe), and the distributions are not statistically distinguishable (Kolmogorov–Smirnov, p>0.05). A real but small hydraulic interference exists — 0.18 bar median pressure reduction at Infiernitos by year 25 — an order of magnitude below natural-state uncertainty.
items.chartCaption: Combined net power output, 25-year forecast, 293-sample ensemble — grey: individual samples; red: P10/P50/P90
items.statsNote: 25-year time-averaged net output across the ensemble (mean 89.3 MWe)
items.source: From our own in-preparation manuscript on Tecuamburro–Infiernitos combined resource assessment — not yet peer-reviewed.

items.title: Momotombo: three decades of reservoir performance and reinjection strategy
items.loc: Momotombo Geothermal Field, Nicaragua · Producing since 1983, 77 MWe installed
items.brief: Build and continually re-calibrate the three-dimensional numerical reservoir model behind one of Central America's longest-producing geothermal fields, across more than three decades of exploitation.
items.challenge: A field in continuous production since 1983 needs its reservoir model re-calibrated against new pressure, tracer and production data as the resource itself evolves — not a one-off build, but a model kept honest for decades.
items.method: Three-dimensional numerical reservoir model construction and calibration; reinjection scheme design based on reservoir-pressure monitoring and tracer-test analysis; production-history review at 23, 25 and 27 years of exploitation.
items.outcome: Updated conceptual and numerical models carried the field's development planning through multiple decades; reinjection strategy informed directly by tracer and pressure-monitoring data rather than assumed.
items.source: Porras, E. et al. — "Numerical modeling of the Momotombo geothermal system, Nicaragua", Proceedings, World Geothermal Congress 2005, and "Reinjection scheme in Momotombo, Nicaragua, on the basis of reservoir pressure monitoring, tracer test analysis and numerical modeling study", Geothermal Resources Council 2007.

items.title: Salton Sea: a 3D natural-state model for one of the world's largest geothermal resources
items.loc: Salton Sea Geothermal Field, California, USA · ~3 GW estimated resource potential
items.brief: Build the first publicly available integrated 3D conceptual and natural-state model of a field that, despite its scale, has only been partially exploited — held back by uniquely high-salinity brine and partial coverage by the Salton Sea itself.
items.challenge: No public numerical model existed for a resource this size, at a moment when a receding shoreline, California's renewable-energy targets and new direct lithium-extraction methods have all renewed interest in developing it further.
items.method: 3D conceptual model built in Leapfrog Geothermal from open-source geology, geophysics and geochemistry data; natural-state model built and calibrated in Waiwera and TOUGH2 against public well-temperature data and surface manifestations; later refined with a chloride-NCG-water equation of state carrying lithium as a passive tracer, and uncertainty-quantified against porosity, permeability and upflow.
items.outcome: A calibrated natural-state model capable of forecasting lithium concentration in produced fluids under direct lithium extraction, and of testing how multiple developers sharing one resource affect each other's production — the same shared-resource question our own Tecuamburro–Infiernitos work asks.
items.source: Araya, N. & O'Sullivan, J. (2022) — Geothermal Resources Council Transactions; Renaud, T., Croucher, A., Dekkers, K., Gravatt, M., O'Sullivan, M., Popineau, J., Riffault, J., Tonkin, R. & O'Sullivan, J. (2025) — Proceedings, 50th Stanford Geothermal Workshop, SGP-TR-229.
